title: Quantitative Analysis and Reproducible Work
answer: Reproducible notebooks, asking data questions in plain language, large-scale compute, statistical code and testing a design before collecting data.

children.name: Reproducible Notebooks and Pipelines
children.blurb: Reproducible notebooks and pipelines are the working documents and workflow definitions that let a quantitative analysis be rerun with the same code, data, environment, and results.

children.name: Asking Data Questions in Plain Language
children.blurb: Asking data questions in plain language covers the practice of querying structured datasets, tables, and documents using natural language instead of formal query code.

children.name: Large-Scale Compute on Institutional Data
children.blurb: Large-scale compute on institutional data refers to running computationally intensive analyses over datasets held by institutions, such as administrative records, research cohorts, operational logs, or survey data.

children.name: Writing Statistical Code with AI
children.blurb: Writing statistical code with AI covers using large language models and code assistants to draft, debug, document, and translate statistical routines in languages such as R, Python, or Stata.

children.name: Testing a Study Design Before Data Collection
children.blurb: Testing a study design before data collection is the practice of using simulation, power analysis, and protocol review to check whether a planned quantitative study can answer its research question.

sections.body: This field covers the practical machinery of quantitative research: making analyses reproducible, turning plain-language questions into data queries, running large computations on institutional data, writing statistical code, and testing study designs before data collection. Artificial intelligence is now doing concrete work in each area. Language models generate notebook cells, refactor pipelines, and suggest documentation for version-controlled workflows. They translate a researcher's sentence like 'compare outcomes by group' into SQL or Python that runs against a real dataset. They also draft simulation code and power calculations for a proposed experiment. This is not theoretical; these tools are used daily to produce actual analysis scripts, logs, and reports.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Reproducible notebooks and pipelines are well supported by AI that can fill in boilerplate, fix dependency errors, and explain a failed run, but the generated code still needs human review because it can silently use the wrong statistical test or mishandle missing data. Asking data questions in plain language works for simple aggregations and joins, yet it degrades quickly on ambiguous terms, nested logic, or domain-specific schemas. Large-scale compute on institutional data is partly solved for orchestration and resource allocation, but AI cannot safely reason about access controls, data governance, or the cost of a distributed job without explicit rules. Writing statistical code with AI is reliable for standard models like linear regression or t-tests, but less so for custom estimators, complex survey weights, or Bayesian workflows. Testing a study design before data collection is promising for generating simulation plans, but the AI does not know whether your assumptions about effect size or dropout are realistic. The honest limit is that these tools accelerate and check work, they do not replace a statistician's judgment.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader should start with Reproducible Notebooks and Pipelines to see how AI helps keep an analysis runnable from raw data to final figure. From there, Asking Data Questions in Plain Language shows how to move from a research question to an actual query without writing code by hand. Large-Scale Compute on Institutional Data then addresses what changes when the data cannot leave a hospital or government server and the computation must be brought to it. Writing Statistical Code with AI narrows the focus to the correctness of the analysis itself, covering how AI drafts, tests, and documents statistical routines. Finally, Testing a Study Design Before Data Collection closes the loop by using AI to simulate the experiment and catch design flaws before any real data is gathered. Together these pages move from environment to question to scale to code to design, which is the order a careful quantitative project actually follows.
